pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5–7; know that many everyday foods come from rainforests — chocolate from cacao beans, bananas, shade-grown coffee, Brazil nuts — and connect their own plate to a faraway forest.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS1 Science 'Plants' (identify and name a variety of plants, including edible plants; know that food comes from plants and animals); KS1 Geography (locate hot places near the Equator, where these foods grow); DT 'where food comes from'.
• Standards — US: NGSS K-ESS3-1 (relationship between needs of organisms—including humans—and where they live) flavour; broader 'plants as a source of food' science-and-social-studies link.
• Operational details — build the FOOD → FOREST-SOURCE mapping concretely: chocolate bar ← cacao pod on a trunk; banana ← tropical banana plant; coffee ← red berries ripening in forest shade; Brazil nut ← giant emergent tree. Start from foods the child actually eats so the link is personal, then trace back to the tree. Emphasise 'grows on a tree/plant in a hot wet place near the Equator', not manufacturing detail.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (5): name two foods that come from the rainforest. Tier B (6): explain that chocolate is made from cacao beans that grow on rainforest trees. Tier C (7): pick a food they ate today and trace it back to a rainforest plant.
bestPractices: Start from the child's own eaten food (a chocolate bar, a banana) and trace BACKWARDS to the tree, so the connection is personal and memorable.
Show the surprising in-between form — the cacao POD split open with beans — to break the assumption that chocolate 'comes from a shop'.
Keep the geography light but real: these plants grow in hot, wet places near the Equator, tying to 'What Is a Rainforest?'.
Use real photos or vivid illustrations of the growing plant, not just the packaged product, to cement the source.
Avoid manufacturing detail (fermenting, roasting) at this age — the learning goal is the food→plant→forest link.
keyRepresentations: A familiar plate/breakfast table of foods (chocolate, banana, coffee, nuts) as the entry point.
The cacao pod on a tree trunk — the iconic 'chocolate really starts here' image.
A simple food→plant pairing card set (product on one side, growing plant on the other).
A world map dot near the Equator showing 'this is where it grows'.
commonMisconceptions: 'Chocolate is made in a factory / comes from a cow' — children conflate the shop or milk with the true plant origin (cacao beans).
'Food comes from the supermarket' — the shop is the end of the chain, not the source.
'Bananas/coffee grow in Britain' — not realising these need hot, wet tropical conditions.
'Nuts grow underground/in packets' — Brazil nuts fall inside heavy pods from giant rainforest trees.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7: children learn that many everyday foods come from rainforests — chocolate from cacao beans, bananas, shade-grown coffee, Brazil nuts — by starting from foods they actually eat and tracing each one backwards to the tree or plant it grew on in a hot, wet place near the Equator. The intended goal is a personal, memorable FOOD → PLANT → FOREST link, not manufacturing detail. The main proposal is a tap-to-zoom breakfast-table image; active matching/sorting and an end-check are preserved as alternatives with distinct purposes.

activities.title: Tap a food, travel back to its rainforest tree
feedback: If the child says chocolate is 'just made in a factory' or 'comes from a cow/milk', trace it back to cacao beans growing in pods on a tree — the factory only processes beans that come from a tree (milk chocolate may also contain milk, but the chocolate itself starts as cacao beans on a plant).
If the child stops the story at the shop ('it comes from the supermarket'), follow one food back past the shop to the plant or forest it grew in; the shop is the end of the chain, not the source.
If the child thinks bananas or coffee grow in Britain, point out these plants need hot, wet tropical conditions near the Equator.

If the child thinks Brazil nuts grow underground or in packets, show Brazil nuts falling inside heavy pods from giant rainforest trees (peanuts really do grow underground, but Brazil nuts grow in pods on trees).

Reinforce correct links by having the child name a second food that comes from a rainforest, say what grows on the cacao tree before it becomes chocolate, and describe how a banana travels from a tropical forest to their lunchbox.
activities.rationale: Starting from the child's own eaten food and tracing backwards to the tree is intended to make the connection personal and memorable, and the surprising in-between form (the split cacao pod with beans) is designed to challenge the assumption that chocolate 'comes from a shop'. Tap-to-zoom drill-down lets each food reveal its growing plant and where it grows, aiming to cement the source with vivid real photos or illustrations rather than the packaged product only. This is a research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention; only the underlying content — that food comes from plants and that these specific foods come from rainforests — is curriculum/botany supported.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils identify and name a variety of common plants including edible plants and learn that food comes from plants and animals
Cacao (chocolate), bananas, coffee and Brazil nuts are among staple foods native to or grown in tropical rainforests
learnerActions: Look at a familiar plate or breakfast table showing foods the child actually eats: a chocolate bar, a banana, a cup of coffee, a handful of Brazil nuts.

First guess the surprise flap question 'Where does chocolate REALLY come from?', then tap the chocolate bar and watch it zoom/flip into a knobbly cacao pod split open on a rainforest tree trunk, spilling pale beans, with the caption 'chocolate begins here, on a tree in a hot, wet forest.'
Tap the banana to travel to a towering tropical banana plant; tap the coffee to find red berries ripening in green forest shade; tap the nuts to see a giant emergent tree drop a heavy seed-pod.
Say aloud for one food: where it grows, that it grows on a tree or plant in a hot wet place near the Equator, and that the shop is the END of the journey, not the start.
Close the pictures, answer the flap question 'Where does chocolate REALLY come from?' from memory, then lift the flap to check your answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Some ordinary foods on my plate, like chocolate, bananas, coffee and Brazil nuts, began their life far away on trees or plants from hot, wet rainforest places, so my breakfast is connected to faraway forests.

activities.title: Match the food to the tree it grew on
feedback: When a match bounces back, prompt the child to look at the growing form again — what does a cacao pod hold, what do coffee berries become?
Praise a correct match by asking the child to recall where that plant grows (a hot, wet place near the Equator).
If the child guesses randomly, slow down and have them name the food first, then hunt for its plant.
activities.rationale: An active drag-to-match game is proposed as engaging for KS1 and may double as light performance evidence, letting children construct the pairings themselves rather than only recognise them. It is slightly more than the minimum the topic needs but offers a hands-on alternative to passive viewing; its comparative effectiveness over the tap-to-zoom image is not established.
learnerActions: Drag each supermarket food (chocolate bar, banana, coffee, Brazil nut) onto the rainforest tree or plant it grew on.
Watch wrong matches bounce back and correct ones trigger a short animation from the growing form (cacao pod with beans, coffee berry, banana bunch, Brazil nut pod) to the food we buy.
After matching, say for one pair why that food belongs to that plant (e.g. 'chocolate comes from cacao beans in a pod on this tree').
activities.intendedInsight: Each everyday food can be paired with the specific rainforest plant it came from, and the growing form (bean, berry, pod) turns into the food we recognise.

activities.title: End check: sort and match rainforest foods
feedback: If the child misclassifies, revisit the specific food's growing plant and where it grows.
If the child can name foods but cannot trace chocolate to cacao beans on a tree, re-walk the cacao pod → beans → chocolate chain.
Encourage connecting a food they personally ate today back to its forest origin to surface the food-to-forest link.
activities.rationale: A sort-and-match check aligns directly with the evidence statements and gives a tidy end-of-topic verification of the edible-plant content KS1 covers. It checks recognition and recall rather than itself building the personal food→forest connection, so it is best used after the tracing activities, not instead of them.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils identify and name a variety of common plants including edible plants and learn that food comes from plants and animals
learnerActions: Sort a set of foods into 'from the rainforest' versus 'not from the rainforest'.
Match each rainforest food to the plant it grows on.
Name at least three foods that come from rainforests, and explain that cacao beans grow on trees in the rainforest and are made into chocolate.
Pick a rainforest food you ate today or recently and trace it back to the plant it grew on.
activities.intendedInsight: I can recognise which everyday foods come from rainforests and explain the chocolate-from-cacao chain.

constraints: Avoid manufacturing detail (fermenting, roasting) at this age — the learning goal is the food→plant→forest link, not how a factory processes beans.
Keep the geography light but real: these plants grow in hot, wet places near the Equator; tie to 'What Is a Rainforest?' without heavy map work.
Use real photos or vivid illustrations of the growing plant, not just the packaged product, so the source is concrete.
The sort/match check verifies recognition and recall; it does not on its own build the personal, memorable food→forest connection, so pair it with the tracing activity rather than replacing it.

A 3D model was judged to add decorative cost with no learning gain for THIS topic because the concept is a set of food–plant associations with no spatial or physics payload; this is a fit judgement here, not a universal claim about 3D.

Open dialogue/persona formats were judged low-value for this simple factual association at ages 5–7; this does not mean conversation cannot teach procedures or concepts, only that it is low-value for this specific objective.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both listed sources are marked verified:false in the row and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The cited source claims are curriculum/botany statements supporting that these foods come from rainforests and that KS1 covers edible plants; they do NOT establish the comparative effectiveness of any specific activity format.
A reteach prerequisite reference for the 'food comes from the supermarket' misconception was carried over unchanged from the assessment field; its validity was not re-checked.

The original row lists 'chocolate comes from a cow/milk' as a child misconception; milk chocolate does contain milk, so the correction focuses on the cacao-bean plant origin rather than denying any dairy involvement, to avoid confusing a child who has seen 'milk chocolate' on a label.

probeDeeper: Name another food that comes from a rainforest.
What grows on the cacao tree before it becomes chocolate?
How does a banana get from a tropical forest to your lunchbox?
assess.correctAnswer: Chocolate starts in the rainforest: it's made from cacao beans that grow in pods on cacao trees in hot, wet tropical forests. The factory turns the beans into chocolate, but the beans come from a tree. Lots of everyday foods — bananas, coffee, Brazil nuts — come from rainforests too, so our food connects us to faraway forests.

errorPatterns.pattern: chocolate comes from a factory (or from cows/milk) — no plant origin
errorPatterns.nextMove: trace it to cacao beans growing in pods on a tree; the factory only processes them
errorPatterns.distractor: It's just made in a factory out of sugar and milk
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says chocolate is just made in a factory or comes from cows

errorPatterns.pattern: food comes from the supermarket, not nature — 'it comes from the shop'
errorPatterns.nextMove: follow one food back past the shop to the plant or forest it grew in
errorPatterns.revealedBy: stops the story at the shop with no natural source

responseLevels.gap: Thinks chocolate/food just comes from a factory or shop, with no natural origin.
responseLevels.full: Explains chocolate comes from cacao beans grown on rainforest trees (processed in a factory), names other rainforest foods, and connects their own eating to faraway forests.
responseLevels.partial: Knows some foods come from plants but can't trace chocolate to cacao beans on a tree, or name other rainforest foods.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Where does chocolate really come from — is it made in a factory out of nothing, or does it start as something growing in a rainforest? Tell me, and then tell me WHY chocolate is connected to rainforests.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks chocolate is 'just made in a factory' misses its forest origin; the concept child traces it back to cacao beans on a tree. The reason-tier surfaces the food-to-forest link.
